2b1e3a4a-e4eb-11f1-b58c-3b71a49c3391.one_liner: Macro Compass/Spectrum Markets hosts argue this selloff mirrors Q4 2018 -- a hawkish Fed (Waller) hiking into deteriorating data risks a credit-issuance freeze and forced capex/deleveraging, with the Fed only reversing after a 2019-style capitulation.
2b1e3a4a-e4eb-11f1-b58c-3b71a49c3391.recap: Alfonso Peccatiello and Brent Donnelly discuss a brutal cross-asset selloff with bonds and stocks falling together, leaving nowhere to hide. Donnelly admits he tried fading the Fed's hawkish turn -- driven by Governor Waller's data-dependent hiking rhetoric amid an internal Fed 'civil war' with Waller reportedly undercutting Governor (Lisa) Cook/others -- and got hurt, though he still believes the Fed's forward guidance lacks credibility. Both draw an extended parallel to Q4 2018: strong prior risk-asset gains, a hawkish Powell declaring policy 'a long way from neutral,' a market selloff that froze corporate bond issuance for months, and a Fed that only reversed after Powell's January 2019 'sorry, sorry, sorry' capitulation. They note a December hike is now fully priced, and argue slowing capex (less ability to issue credit/equity when spreads widen and stocks are down) becomes self-reinforcing, lowering growth and eventually forcing the Fed's hand -- citing the RBA's pivot from hiking to pricing March cuts as a live template. They discuss dollar mechanics (hedger rebalancing then a later reversal as capital repatriates, e.g., to Switzerland), a correlation trade combining USD/CHF downside with S&P downside (dual-digital option, mispriced at near-zero correlation), and note gold/silver/Bitcoin are trading as liquidity proxies rather than hedges, having given back much of their 2025 breakout gains. Donnelly closes less bearish than the conversation sounds, estimating 70-80% of the move is done but stressing path risk.
terms: OIS -- Overnight Index Swap, used to gauge expected central bank policy rates

461a68a7-c4bd-4b0d-820b-28504a672614.recap: Chris Whalen (Institutional Risk Analyst) argues Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has lost market credibility by talking tough on inflation without acting, unlike Paul Volcker. Whalen says the Fed should have hiked in steady quarter-point steps all year and widened the Fed funds/reserve-interest spread to signal balance-sheet intent; instead it waited on task forces while long-term yields rose roughly 4.5 points, pushing the system near its practical upper bound. He stresses that money markets run on spreads, not absolute rates -- repo funding cost versus asset yield is what matters -- and that economists like Chris Waller underweight this. Whalen's biggest near-term worry is mortgages: falling refinance volumes (toward 20-25% of total) starve non-bank lenders of liquidity, MSRs are flipping from negative to positive duration (Ellington sold its whole MSR book), rental/business-purpose and second-lien lending is deteriorating, and Fitch downgraded issuers. He separately warns that SEC/Fed-driven mandatory central clearing for Treasury cash and repo (deadlines pushed to December/next July) will reduce foreign and dealer demand for Treasuries just as issuance surges (~$800bn January refunding), evoking the March 2020 dash-for-cash. He also flags commercial real estate walk-aways (Brookfield), weak IPO reception (Anthropic), gold/copper weakness tied to higher real rates, and views equity rotation into bonds as a warning sign for high-yield and consumer-facing credit into 2027.
terms: MSR -- Mortgage Servicing Right, the right to service a mortgage loan in exchange for a fee, typically a negative-duration asset that gains value as rates rise

4a037da0-75bc-471d-bce2-298f33090895.recap: The commentator argues the market narrative blaming the AI/equity selloff on 'higher rates raising the discount rate' is wrong. The real signal was already in the yield curve's shape: steep from bills to the 2-year, but flat from the 2-year out to the 10-year. The front end reflects Fed policy expectations -- here, a hawkish response to energy-driven inflation fears (one hike delivered, another possible in December) -- while the back end reflects the market's own view of growth, inflation and labor-market durability, and it never confirmed an AI-driven reflation. Supporting evidence: 10-year TIPS breakevens just hit a two-year low, undercutting the idea that rising yields reflect inflationary reflation; copper and silver are being liquidated despite tight supply, which the host treats as a real-economy check on AI capex demand; and a fresh divergence has opened between Treasury bills (pricing further Fed hikes) and term SOFR (pricing doubt the Fed can follow through), which he reads as the market disagreeing with hawks like Waller and resilience-callers like Warsh. Anthropic's IPO, despite a spectacular +34%/+17% debut, failed to revive risk appetite -- over 90% of the S&P fell the same day, the Dow dropped 1,100+ points -- and EM equities (MSCI EM down ~3%, near a bear market) and Asian indices (Taiwan's TAIEX down ~18% on the week, KOSPI down 5%+) extended a broad, globally correlated de-risking. His conclusion: the AI boom may be real long-term, but the curve and commodities show the economy lacks the credit/labor resilience to validate current risk-taking near-term.

59d6e207-f957-4c9a-9098-aca4f9169b5f.one_liner: A housing-crash-without-foreclosures narrative that feeds directly into the rates trader's Fed-pivot and wealth-effect thesis, even though it has no repo/collateral content.
59d6e207-f957-4c9a-9098-aca4f9169b5f.recap: The host argues the US housing market is crashing in activity, not yet in price, and that this is structurally different from 2008. Pending home sales fell 4.7% in October, down 18% over six months, the lowest level since the NAR began tracking in 2001 and weaker than both 2008 and the pandemic. Every major region declined, led by the West (-6.9%) and South (-6.3%); the national index is down roughly 17% year-over-year. Redfin data show only 3 of the 50 largest metros remain seller's markets (tying the record low from April 2020), with sellers outnumbering buyers by 70.5% nationally for a sixth straight record month, and only about 895,752 buyers in the market, the lowest since 2013. Housing starts rose but almost entirely via noisy multifamily supply; single-family permits fell to a nearly four-year low, signaling builders expect weak demand ahead. The core argument: this isn't 2008's forced-selling, foreclosure-driven price collapse, because most homeowners hold cheap fixed-rate mortgages and aren't distressed sellers. Instead, buyers are vanishing because households doubt future income and job security, not just because of mortgage rates. The host ties this to the yield curve's current shape (steep front, flat back) and unmoved swap spreads, arguing bond markets already doubt the Fed's hawkish persistence, echoing late 2023 before the 2024 slowdown. If home prices start falling even modestly, the reversal of the housing wealth effect could further weaken an already fragile consumer and push the Fed toward cuts in 2026.

caba60ee-e48f-11f1-899a-9375cafeb724.recap: Hosts on Forward Guidance discuss the Anthropic IPO (pricing at ~$2 trillion, aggressive unlock schedule, heavy retail demand) as emblematic of AI-trade exhaustion: token prices are collapsing even as usage rises, squeezing frontier-model margins. They tie this to Nvidia's ~40% drawdown and note credit markets have effectively closed to data center/neocloud financing, forcing reliance on equity raises instead of unsecured debt — a reversal of the 'circular financing' dynamic that propped up hyperscaler capex. On rates, they argue the Fed is behind the curve: FOMC minutes this week flagged AI-driven inflation risk just as the AI build-out is visibly slowing, and hawkish rhetoric from regional Fed presidents (Waller floating 50bp hike odds) is keeping bonds from rallying even as equal-weight equities, housing starts, and commodities (oil down 35%, copper weak per Druckenmiller) all signal a broadening slowdown. They note real rates are near GFC-era highs after the Fed reversed heavy repo/liquidity operations ($40bn/month) earlier in the year. Comparisons are drawn to 2018 (weak labor market, policy mistake risk) versus 2022 (inflation overshoot), concluding current conditions combine the worst of both. Treasury's Bessent is notably absent after a year of active market intervention. They argue a slow, controlled 'bleed' rather than a V-shaped crash is needed to actually durably lower inflation, and expect gold/Bitcoin and duration trades to wait until slowdown confirmation.
